body:
Keep the cause, location and result together

India's major security conflicts since independence can be distinguished by who fought, where the fighting occurred and what followed. A year alone is often insufficient because several wars and agreements are connected across different years.

ConflictPrincipal location or issueImmediate result or follow-up
1947–48Jammu and KashmirCeasefire effective in January 1949; Karachi Agreement in July 1949
1962Aksai Chin and NEFAChinese unilateral ceasefire in November 1962; boundary dispute unresolved
1965Kutch, Jammu and Kashmir, PunjabSeptember 1965 ceasefire; Tashkent Declaration in January 1966
1971East Pakistan and the India–Pakistan frontsSurrender at Dhaka; Bangladesh's independence; Simla Agreement in July 1972
1999Kargil region along the LoCRecovery of occupied positions through Operation Vijay

Match historical figures with their exact roles

The same war may involve a Prime Minister, an Army Chief, a field commander and a foreign leader. Their roles should not be treated as equivalent.

PersonAssociated eventPrecisely identified role
Maharaja Hari Singh1947Signed Jammu and Kashmir's Instrument of Accession
Jawaharlal Nehru1962Prime Minister of India during the China war
V. K. Krishna Menon1962Defence Minister who resigned during the war
Lal Bahadur Shastri1965–66Prime Minister during the 1965 War; signed Tashkent
Ayub Khan1966President of Pakistan; signed Tashkent
Indira Gandhi1971–72Prime Minister during the 1971 War; signed Simla
Yahya Khan1971Headed Pakistan's military government during the war
Sam Manekshaw1971India's Chief of the Army Staff
A. A. K. Niazi1971Pakistani Eastern Commander who signed the surrender
Jagjit Singh Aurora1971Indian commander who accepted the surrender at Dhaka
Zulfikar Ali Bhutto1972President of Pakistan; signed Simla

Different dates can describe different stages of one event

Several dates belong to the same historical sequence. The 26 October 1947 accession preceded the 27 October acceptance and troop landing. The 1965 ceasefire preceded the 1966 Tashkent Declaration. The 16 December 1971 surrender preceded the 2 July 1972 Simla Agreement.

This pattern helps explain why an answer may be historically related to a question but still be incorrect. A question asking for the date of a surrender is not asking for the date of the subsequent peace agreement.

High-value paired distinctions

  • Tashkent versus Simla: 1966, Shastri and Ayub Khan, after the 1965 War; versus 1972, Indira Gandhi and Bhutto, after the 1971 War.
  • Niazi versus Aurora: Niazi signed the surrender for Pakistani forces; Aurora accepted it on behalf of the Indian and Bangladesh forces.
  • Manekshaw versus Aurora: Manekshaw was India's Army Chief; Aurora was the Indian commander at the Dhaka surrender.
  • Aksai Chin versus Kargil: Aksai Chin was central to the 1962 India–China dispute; Kargil was the site of the 1999 India–Pakistan conflict.
  • Ceasefire Line versus LoC: The former was established through the 1949 Karachi arrangements; the latter was recognised in the 1972 Simla Agreement.
  • Gujarat versus Bangladesh connection: The Rann of Kutch was associated with the 1965 conflict; the liberation of East Pakistan and surrender at Dhaka were associated with 1971.

Prelims focus

  • 1947 accession: Hari Singh; 1949 ceasefire-line agreement: Karachi.
  • 1962: China, Aksai Chin and NEFA.
  • 1965: Kutch and Kashmir; 1966: Tashkent, Shastri and Ayub Khan.
  • 1971: Dhaka, Niazi and Aurora; 1972: Simla, Indira Gandhi and Bhutto.
  • 1999: Kargil, Operation Vijay and 26 July.
  • Trap: Match every person to the precise role performed, not merely to the war with which the person is associated.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 8, Our Pasts–III, 2020–21, Chapter 10, 'India After Independence', printed pp. 128–129; NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India since Independence, Chapter 4, 'India's External Relations', printed pp. 68–76; NCERT, Class 12, Contemporary World Politics, Chapter 5, 'Contemporary South Asia', printed pp. 68–71; United Nations Treaty Series, Volume 81, No. 1076, Karachi Agreement, 27 July 1949; United Nations Treaty Series, Volume 560, No. 8166, Tashkent Declaration, 10 January 1966; Ministry of External Affairs, Government of India, Simla Agreement, 2 July 1972, clauses 1–6; Government of India, Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, 1971 victory commemorative-stamp release, 16 December 2021, and Kargil Vijay Diwas release, 26 July 2018; online documents consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A chronological timeline links five conflicts to military outcomes and distinguishes the later Karachi, Tashkent and Simla agreements.
pictures.caption: The complete sequence of conflicts, ceasefires and major agreements from 1947 to 1999.

title: One-Glance Prelims Revision: Wars, Leaders, Commanders and Agreements
